articles.title: Hopwood Hall College celebrates topping out of new Clegg Building
articles.excerpt: A topping out ceremony at Hopwood Hall College marks a significant step in the construction of the new Clegg Building, set to enhance educational facilities in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
A topping out ceremony was held at Hopwood Hall College on October 26, 2026, marking a significant milestone in the construction of the new Clegg Building. This event celebrated the completion of the building's structure, which is being developed by Willmott Dixon and funded by the Department for Education, Rochdale Council, and the college itself.

The ceremony was attended by notable figures including Principal and CEO Julia Heap OBE, Rochdale MP Paul Waugh, and the Mayor and Mayoress of Rochdale, Faisal Rana and Iram Faisal. Family members of the late Robert Clegg OBE, after whom the building is named, were also present, highlighting the personal connection to the college. Robert Clegg served as Chair of the Corporation from 2007 to 2018 and made significant contributions during his tenure.

During the event, attendees were taken to the roof of the new building, which offers panoramic views of the borough, including landmarks such as Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Parish Church. Guests were invited to leave messages on the roof parapet, creating a lasting record of the occasion.

The Clegg Building is expected to provide a modern and inspiring learning environment for students at Hopwood Hall College, enhancing educational opportunities in the area. As construction progresses, the college community looks forward to the completion of this landmark development, which aims to foster a better learning experience for current and future students.

Littleborough Rugby Club faced Trafford MV in a challenging match in the ADM Lancs/Cheshire 2 league on Saturday, October 26, 2026. The match took place at Littleborough's home ground, where the team managed to secure a win despite adverse weather conditions, including heavy rain and strong winds.

Trafford MV entered the game with a number of key players unavailable due to injuries, which affected their performance. They initially took the lead with a try from Mica Dyos, making the score 5-0. However, Littleborough responded quickly, scoring a try and converting it to lead 7-5 at half-time.

This victory keeps Littleborough at the top of the league, while Trafford MV slips further down the standings. The match highlights the challenges teams face during adverse weather conditions and the impact of player availability on performance.

articles.title: 34 foster families recognised for dedication at Rochdale Town Hall awards
articles.excerpt: At an awards ceremony in Rochdale Town Hall, 34 foster families were honoured for their commitment to caring for vulnerable children, collectively fostering for 465 years.
articles.content_html:
Thirty-four foster families were honoured at the annual Foster Carer Celebration Awards held at Rochdale Town Hall, recognising their dedication to providing safe and nurturing homes for vulnerable children. Collectively, these families have fostered for an impressive 465 years, supporting over 1,020 children and young people from newborns to 18 years old.

Among those celebrated were Michael and Marilyn, a couple from Milnrow, who have fostered for 50 years since 1976. They have cared for over 330 children, primarily focusing on newborns and siblings. Marilyn expressed her love for fostering, stating, "How long is a piece of string?" when asked how long they would continue. She reflected on the joy of seeing children grow up and receiving letters from adoptive parents thanking them for their influence.

The event highlighted the vital role foster families play in the community, providing stability and care to those in need. The awards serve not only to recognise the individual contributions of these families but also to raise awareness about the importance of fostering in Rochdale.

This recognition is significant as it underscores the ongoing need for foster carers in the area. With many children still in need of stable homes, the event aims to inspire others in the community to consider fostering. For those interested in becoming foster carers, further information can be obtained from the local authority's fostering service.

articles.title: Heywood nursery loses planning bid to keep caravan as outbuilding
articles.excerpt: Little Oaks Nursery in Heywood has been denied permission to retain a caravan used as an outbuilding, following a planning decision by Rochdale Council.
articles.content_html:
Little Oaks Nursery, located on Bamford Road in Heywood, has lost its bid to keep a caravan that replaced a temporary Portakabin in its yard. The nursery applied for retrospective planning permission for the caravan, which has been used as an outbuilding since the Portakabin was removed in 2024 after being granted temporary permission in 2022.

A report from a planning officer indicated that pre-application advice had been sought regarding the placement of a static caravan on the site. The advice stated that such a structure would not be visually appropriate and would be highly visible from both directions along Bamford Road. Despite this, the caravan was placed on the site without the necessary planning permission, prompting the nursery's application to regulate its presence.

The planning officer's report further noted that the caravan does not meet the high-quality design standards required for a permanent structure. It was concluded that the caravan does not offer any visual improvement over the temporary Portakabin it replaced, which was only accepted for a limited time due to its unsuitability for permanent retention.

This decision by Rochdale Council highlights ongoing concerns regarding planning regulations and the visual impact of structures within the area. Local residents and businesses may be affected by the enforcement of these regulations, as they aim to maintain the aesthetic integrity of the neighbourhood.

Monday 26 October: Afternoon tea at Denehurst Café runs from 12.30pm to 2.30pm. Booking is required, so contact GTAS to check availability before attending.

Wednesday 28 October: The Remembrance and Reflection Walk offers a gentle amble around the park, with time to chat and reflect. Meet at Denehurst Café at 12.15pm, ready for a 12.30pm start. Sunday 1 November: GTAS Men’s Sunday League kicks off at 11am, with the venue still to be confirmed. GTAS Ladies are listed at Saddleworth 3Ds FC with a 3.30pm kick off.

The programme offers opportunities to spend time with others locally, whether over tea, on a walk or through sport. articles.title: Rochdale Council Tax Direct Debits delayed by one day after system error
articles.excerpt: Council Tax Direct Debits due on Monday 26 October will instead be collected on Tuesday 27 October, Rochdale Council says. The notice applies to the affected collection date.
articles.content_html:
Residents whose Rochdale Council Tax Direct Debit was due to leave their account on Monday 26 October 2026 should expect it to be collected on Tuesday 27 October instead, following a system error at the council.

The authority has placed a notice across its official website explaining that payments scheduled for Monday 26 October will be taken one day later. It has not said in that notice how many accounts are affected, what caused the error or whether any other collection dates will change. The published change concerns this specific Monday collection date, not every Council Tax instalment.

For residents who budget closely around outgoing payments, the practical point is to leave enough money in the account for the revised Tuesday collection. A payment not showing as taken on Monday does not, by itself, mean the instalment has been cancelled. Residents should avoid making an additional manual payment simply because the usual Direct Debit has not yet appeared, without first checking their account or speaking to the council.

The council says residents can check their Council Tax balance through its MyAccount service. People who need help can contact the Council Tax team on 0300 303 8870. These are official council channels; no bank details should be supplied to an unsolicited caller or message claiming to be about the delay.

The notice was checked on Monday 26 October. It does not explain whether customers will receive individual notifications. Rochdale Daily will update this report if the council announces any further change.

Official information: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/counciltax. Council Tax account guidance: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax/council-tax-account-balance-enquiries. Council contact details: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/contactcentre.

articles.title: Wednesday deadline to comment on parking changes in Rochdale, Littleborough and Milnrow
articles.excerpt: Residents have until Wednesday 28 October to comment on three proposed parking orders affecting Mere Street, Wardle Street and the Butterworth Hall area.
articles.content_html:
Drivers and residents have until Wednesday 28 October 2026 to object to or comment on three proposed parking restriction changes across Rochdale borough. The council has published notices of intent for Mere Street in Rochdale, Wardle Street in Littleborough and the Butterworth Hall and Royds Street area in Milnrow. These are proposals, not restrictions already in force.

On Mere Street, near Drake Street in the Milkstone and Deeplish ward, the proposal would shorten existing no waiting at any time restrictions on both sides of the road from 22 metres to 15 metres from the junction. That would release a small additional length for parking. The council says the change follows the introduction of one way working and pavement build outs, and is intended to improve local parking provision without compromising visibility. The order reference is H60/1456.

On Wardle Street in Littleborough, the council proposes new no waiting at any time restrictions on the north side for 10 metres from Whitelees Road, and on the south side between Whitelees Road and Frederick Street. Its stated reasons include junction visibility, narrow carriageway width and reports of vehicles parking on both sides or on the footway. The reference is H60/1457.

In Milnrow, the Butterworth Hall area proposal would introduce no waiting at any time restrictions on the south side of Butterworth Hall for 59 metres from Royds Street, and on the east side of Royds Street for 24 metres from Butterworth Hall. The council cites double parking and difficulties for refuse and other larger vehicles using the roads. The reference is H60/1459. The notice's heading labels the amendment as 2027, while its objection deadline is explicitly 28 October 2026; readers should use the council's order reference when asking for clarification.

Comments or objections must reach the council by 28 October. Residents can email trafficorders@rochdale.gov.uk or write to Network Management, Floor 2, Number One Riverside, Smith Street, Rochdale OL16 1XU, stating the relevant reference and the reasons for their objection. The council also accepts comments in support while the objection period is open.

The full notices, maps and reasons are available through the council's Traffic Regulation Orders page: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/roadworks-repairs-restrictions/proposed-permanent-restrictions-highways-traffic-regulation-orders.

Would these proposals make your street safer, or make parking more difficult? Share your experience in the comments. Do not assume a proposal is already enforceable until the council confirms the final order.

articles.title: New book showcases unseen 1930s photographs of Rochdale's Norden Riviera
articles.excerpt: A new book featuring 600 unseen photographs captures the essence of 1930s Rochdale, including the lost Norden Riviera lido, highlighting the area's historical significance during a transformative decade.
articles.content_html:
A new book titled "Britain in the 1930s" by Steven Brindle and Maureen Hill features 600 previously unseen photographs, including images of Rochdale's lost Norden Riviera lido. This collection captures the essence of Greater Manchester on the brink of World War II, showcasing the stark contrasts of the era.

The Norden Riviera, which opened in 1935, was a popular outdoor swimming pool located off Edenfield Road in Norden. It provided a seaside experience for local families who could not afford to travel far. The facility included diving boards, slides, and spectator stands, surrounded by gardens and sports fields, making it a cherished local attraction during the 1930s.

The book highlights the economic challenges faced by the north of England during this decade, with unemployment rates soaring due to the decline of traditional industries. However, it also reflects a time of joy and resilience, as communities sought leisure and enjoyment amidst the hardships of the Great Depression and the aftermath of World War I.

"Britain in the 1930s" is available for £50 and covers various regions, including parts of the old Lancashire, now Greater Manchester. The inclusion of Rochdale's Norden Riviera serves to illustrate the area's rich history and the importance of preserving local heritage.

Manchester, on Boxing Day 1938 Add to preferred sources Comments News Neal Keeling Chief reporter 05:53, 26 Oct 2026 Storm clouds were gathering again globally. But on Boxing Day 1938 she captured, vivaciously, just one aspect of that decade. Crimson-lipped the cashier of the Ritz Dancing Hall in Manchester reflected the population's determination to find joy after the dark days of the First World War, the Great Depression, and unemployment. The 1930s led novelist and broadcaster JB Priestley to his famous vision of "three Englands" – the ancient country of cathedrals and villages, the blackened and scarred industrial Britain created by the Victorians, and the Americanised new consumer world of suburbs, cinemas and motorcars. He came to the conclusion after travelling the country with his suitcase and a typewriter to find material for his book "English Journey" published in 1934. ‌ Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter The decade in Britain saw a nation in transition. The north was hit hard by economic turmoil with unemployment levels soaring above the national average due to the collapse of industries like coal mining and shipbuilding. However, seaside cities became alive in the 1930s, thanks to the expansion of cheap rail travel and the emerging concept of paid holidays with thousands of working-class families flooding to the coast during their “Wakes Weeks” But the south and the midlands had seen a growth in new industries, notably car making, and electrical goods, and were able to withstand the economic fallout which the book says were distributed in a "grotesquely uneven way". ‌ A picture of a young, very well dressed couple, on Oxford Street, London, shows how affluence thrived in parts of the country while elsewhere, like the Lancashire George Orwell (pen name for Eric Blair) discovered in his travelogue "The Road to Wigan Pier" working class communities were decimated by the decline of traditional industries. View 8 Images A Wigan street decorated with washing, 1930s. The land as a place of marked contrasts is captured in a new book, Britain in the 1930s by Steven Brindle and Maureen Hill from Atlantic Publishing, price £50. It features 600 unseen black and white historic photographs of the UK. Counties covered by the book include parts of the old Lancashire, which are now in Greater Manchester, Cheshire, Yorkshire, Lancashire, and Northumberland. ‌ Images include an outdoor swimming pool in Rochdale in 1936 known as the Norden Riviera; soldiers clearing snow from the Manchester to Sheffield railway line; and a busy Deansgate in December 1930. A now lost Rochdale lido gave Mancunians a chance to enjoy a seaside experience without having to travel to the coast or abroad. The Norden Riviera opened in 1935 during when open air swimming was booming in Britaian. Located just off Edenfield Road in Norden, it was 'Rochdale by the sea' for many who could not afford a longer journey or who preferred something nearer to home. The pool was heated and came equipped with diving boards, slides and spectator stands. It was surrounded by attractive gardens, a cafe, a sports field with horse riding facilities, fences for show jumping, cricket pitches and areas for ball games. ‌ View 8 Images The "Rochdale Riviera" - the open air pool as it was at Norden in 1936. The Manchester Guardian newspaper on August 17, 1935. described the facility. It said: "The Norden pool, which measures 80ft by 40ft and is from 2ft 6in deep to 9ft deep is situated in the grounds of what, before the war, was Tenter House, just beyond the bleachworks at Norden, and the stables, where horses are kept for hire, belonged to this residence." "It is surrounded by green deckchairs and by an outdoor café, where one may have tea (or other meals) under green and yellow umbrellas. All around are delightful woods, beyond which one can see a shoulder of hill - but not the three factory chimneys lower down the valley. "A round paddling-pool satisfies the children too young to swim, and the conservatory of the old house has been turned into a ballroom. Next season, tennis courts, a gymnasium, a miniature golf course, and a children's playground will be added to the attractions of the Norden Riviera. ‌ View 8 Images A well-dressed couple in Oxford Street in 1932. "Bathing in the warmed water often continues till late by the light of powerful electric lamps." Other images in the book include Manchester's Cenotaph in St Peter's Square in 1935 in its original location before it was dismantled and reconstructed by Manchester City Council in 2014 at the northeast corner of the square next to the town hall to make way for the expansion of the Metrolink tram service. The memorial was first unveiled on July 12th 1924 by the Earl of Derby assisted by a Mrs Bingle, a local resident, whose three sons all died in the First World War. ‌ View 8 Images Manchester's Cenotaph in St Peter's Square pictured in 1935. A street in Wigan is pictured decorated with washing strung out across it. A Liverpool policeman directing traffic is seen standing in a protector box. These days the East Lancashire Road can be a notorious spot for traffic chaos. But a 1933 picture of the then "Liverpool to South East Lancashire Road" shows just eight vehicles over a half mile distance. The 27 mile highway was built at a cost of £3m. Britain was on the cusp of change in the 1930s. A world that would soon be transformed forever by the Second World War. ‌ Photographs in the book cover every county and city at that time, revealing a nation poised between tradition and modernity. View 8 Images A busy Deansgaate, Manchester in December 1930 The 1930s marked the golden age of the British seaside. Packed beaches, bustling promenades, pleasure piers and elegant hotels lured millions. Blackpool and Morecambe became synonymous with summer holidays. Camping, walking and boating holidays grew in popularity, while lidos, dance halls and pavilion theatres reflected a new culture of recreation and entertainment. ‌ Beyond the towns and cities, much of rural Britain appeared little changed from previous centuries. Medieval market squares, village greens and ancient churches dominated the landscape, while agricultural shows, livestock markets and seasonal fairs continued to shape everyday life. The decade was a world where horses and carts still shared roads with motorcars, and where quaint picturesque villages, market towns and centuries-old buildings remained at the heart of British identity. Co-author, Steven Brindle, is an historian and conservationist from Blackburn. He studied History at Oxford and spent almost forty years with English Heritage in a variety of roles as a historian and Inspector of Ancient Monuments. He has published extensively on architectural and engineering history. The photographs in the collection are from the archive of Associated Newspapers, plus contrbutions from many distinguished photographers. ‌ View 8 Images Holidaymakers on the sea front in Blackpool 1930s. They include: James Dixon-Scott, a photographer who wanted to record landscapes and ways of life that he felt were vanishing. He travelled around Britain taking pictures of buildings and rural scenes with exceptional compositions. Anthony Frank Kersting was a leading British architectural photographer. He was a Londoner who studied at Dulwich College where he developed his creative interests. His work featured a wide range of subjects from industrial landscapes to village life across the country. He was one of the leading architectural photographers of his generation and a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. Will F Taylor was known for photographing sweeping panoramic landscapes across Britain from the end of the Victorian period right through the 1930s. His work has featured in many social history collections. ‌ The book is published on November 5th. View 8 Images The book Britain In The 1930s will be published on November 5th. articles.title: New documentary explores the history of Hollingworth Lake
articles.excerpt: A new YouTube documentary delves into the fascinating history of Hollingworth Lake, revealing its origins and significance to the local community.
articles.content_html:
Hollingworth Lake, a popular recreational area for residents of Oldham, Rochdale, and surrounding regions, has been the subject of a new YouTube documentary that explores its intriguing history. Created by Malc Grimwood, a local history enthusiast, the documentary is part of his channel "Tales From Trails Around The Dales."

The lake, situated on the outskirts of Littleborough beneath the Pennine hills, is a man-made body of water that was established during the Industrial Revolution to support the extensive canal network. Grimwood highlights the lake's significance, stating, "Hollingworth Lake is one of Rochdale's most cherished and well-known beauty spots, offering an escape and a place to enjoy its open spaces and rural setting."

The documentary not only sheds light on the lake's origins but also aims to connect viewers with the natural beauty and historical context of the area. It showcases the surrounding countryside, wooded slopes, and moorland that contribute to the lake's charm and appeal.

For those interested in local history and the environment, the documentary serves as an engaging resource. It invites viewers to appreciate the rich heritage of Hollingworth Lake and encourages them to explore the area, fostering a deeper connection with this beloved landmark.

Marilyn expressed her desire to continue fostering, highlighting the joy and fulfilment it brings to their lives.

The ceremony included heartfelt letters from adoptive parents, expressing gratitude for the care and support provided by the foster carers. These testimonials underscored the vital role that foster carers play in the community and the positive influence they have on the lives of children and families.

This recognition not only honours the individual foster carers but also raises awareness about the importance of fostering in Rochdale. The council encourages anyone interested in becoming a foster carer to reach out and learn more about the process, as there is always a need for dedicated individuals to provide loving homes for children.

A total of 34 fostering families were honoured at the council’s recent annual Foster Carer Celebration Awards at Rochdale Town Hall in gratitude for their outstanding commitment to providing safe, stable and nurturing homes for some of the most vulnerable. Between all the carers, it is estimated they have supported more than 1,020 children and young people from newborn to 18, while working with the local authority. Among those celebrating their individual milestones was Michael, aged 79, and Marilyn, aged 75, who are marking an incredible 50 years. Predominantly caring for newborn babies and siblings since 1976, the married couple from Milnrow have cared for more than 330 children in that time with no signs yet of them slowing down. “How long is a piece of string?” Marilyn joked when asked how long she will continue to foster for, before adding she would really miss fostering. "We’ve been to their weddings, adoption parties, christenings, 18th and 21st birthday parties. “It’s lovely when you think you started off with them as a baby and now, they’ve grown. “We’ve had letters from adoptive parents saying, ‘They’ve turned out like they have because of you’ which is nice.” Adding to their reflection as foster carers, Michael said: “We feel privileged and proud.” Ian (right) and Carole McLean (left) celebrate 40 years of fostering with Rochdale Borough Council. Another couple who have kindly dedicated their lives to providing a safe and stable home to those who need it the most, is Carole, aged (65) and Ian (67) McLean from Rochdale, who are celebrating 40 years. Looking back at their own experience as foster carers, Ian said: “When the children do go, they always take something with them of us because we give them that stability, assistance and support. “We even give them support when they’ve gone and we’ve got a number of former foster children that we class as family and they call us mum and dad, I’ve even given 2 of them away at their weddings.” Among many more memorable moments they have shared as foster carers, Carole was also the birthing partner to another former foster child, an experience she simply described as being ‘brilliant’ to be a part of. In the 4 decades they have provided care, they have supported more than 200 children in total. Richard (left) and Susan Shaw (right) retire from fostering with Rochdale Borough Council after 25 years. Other special milestones celebrated during the event included Richard and Susan Shaw, who are retiring as foster carers after 25 years. Speaking after the recent celebration event, Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, added: "Our foster carers make an extraordinary difference to the lives of children and young people across our borough every single day and ‘Thank you’ simply isn’t a big enough expression for how grateful we are to them. “The dedication, compassion and commitment shown by these families is truly inspiring, and these awards are an opportunity to recognise and celebrate everything they do. "Whether they have been fostering for a few years or several decades, each and every one of them has helped provide the stability, care and support that children need to thrive. “On behalf of Rochdale Borough Council, I would like to thank all our foster carers for the life-changing contribution they make to our communities." Anyone over the age of 21 with a spare room in their home can become a foster carer and support those most in need. articles.title: Free benefits checks at Littleborough and Wardle libraries on Monday and Tuesday
articles.excerpt: Council advisers will offer free, no booking needed benefits checks at Littleborough Library on 26 October and Wardle Library on 27 October, from 10am to noon.
articles.content_html:
Residents unsure whether they are receiving all the financial support available to them can speak to council advisers at two free library drop in sessions this week. The sessions are particularly relevant to pensioners, carers, disabled residents and people worried about household costs, but the council says they are open to adults generally.

The first is at Littleborough Library in Hare Hill Park, Littleborough OL15 9HE, on Monday 26 October 2026 from 10am until noon. The second takes place at Wardle Library, 448 Birch Road, Wardle OL12 9LH, on Tuesday 27 October, also from 10am until noon. No appointment is needed for either event.

The council says advisers can check potential entitlement to Pension Credit, explain Attendance Allowance, review Council Tax Support eligibility and give information about Winter Fuel Payments, Blue Badge applications and other cost of living assistance. They can also signpost residents to organisations offering further help, including Citizens Advice and Age UK. Attending does not guarantee entitlement to a benefit or an immediate payment: decisions depend on the relevant eligibility rules and application process.

Anyone attending is asked to bring details of their income, pensions, savings and benefits already received, so advisers can offer a more accurate check. Those visiting on behalf of a family member should bring relevant information if available. Take care with personal documents and give sensitive details only to the advisers at the official session.

Both sessions are advertised by Rochdale Borough Council as free and do not require booking. Anyone unable to attend can use the council's published events information to find its contact details and check for other advice sessions.
